1:
The heading raises questions of authorship. Keil and Delitzsch report that the genuineness of this prophecy has been impugned by the newer criticism, some refusing it to Jeremiah altogether and others treating it as an interpolation; they name its defenders, one of whom concluded that it contains nothing Jeremiah could not have written in the fourth year of Zedekiah, and that it is as much his work as the oracles against the other nations. Charles Ellicott works on the phrase by the hand of Jeremiah, which occurs only once elsewhere and probably means the prophecy was written by the prophet himself and not dictated. Adam Clarke dates it to the same year and supposes these two chapters were put together, with additions, out of the roll then sent to the captives.

John Calvin explains why the oracle stands where it does. The prophet had been announcing judgment on the neighbouring nations, which was some comfort, but a small one, since it is no great relief to have companions in misery; and the Jews might have objected that they were still buried as in a perpetual grave while the monarchy that held them flourished. So this comes at the end of the book, to tell them the tyranny was not to be perpetual. Matthew Henry notices a harder point, that the king of Babylon had been very kind to Jeremiah and is told of his ruin all the same: the prophets of God must not be governed by favour or affection, and whoever our friends may be, if they are enemies of God we dare not speak peace to them.

On the piling up of imperatives Calvin asks what the heap of words is for, and answers that the faithful had to raise their thoughts above the world to believe a thing then judged incredible, since Babylon ruled the East, the Persians were far off in their mountains, and the Medes were sunk in luxury and reckoned half men. Ellicott would render it a signal rather than a standard, not a rallying point for an army but a means of rapid communication, like the chain of beacon-fires at the opening of a Greek tragedy. Whether the two names that follow are two gods divides them. John Wesley, Henry and Clarke take them for the two principal idols of the place. Ellicott says the inscriptions make them names of one and the same deity, and traces the first in the names of the two great walls of the city. Calvin says plainly that he does not know why some think the second an idol at all: the first he grants was the figment the Babylonians trusted in, but the second he takes for a king well known to the Jews, so that the verse announces the ruin of city, god and throne together.

Calvin observes that since the verb used of the first name means confounded, the second should be rendered terrified rather than broken, and that one of the words for images properly means labour, pointing at the pains of the men who made them; Ellicott would invert the two words, the first meaning sculptured pillars and the second blocks. On the nation out of the north the voices agree and widen. John Gill makes it the Medes and Persians, one nation under Cyrus, lying north of Babylon, Cyrus coming down through Assyria. Clarke says the Medes formed the chief part of that army, and that this war began the disasters which left the country a solitude whose site is now unknown. Ellicott finds it significant that the phrase once used of the danger threatening Judah from Babylon is now turned against Babylon itself, as though the prophet watched one quarter of the sky and saw storm after storm break southward; and both he and Henry reach for the same parallel, the northern tribes that brought down Rome.
4:
How far the promise reaches divides them. John Wesley keeps it literal: when God begins to judge Babylon, in the time of Cyrus, Judah comes out of captivity and some of Israel, hearing their brethren are gone, come up from the places the Assyrians had scattered them to. John Gill says the prophecy cannot be restrained to the literal city, and argues from the fifth verse: asking the way to Zion does not suit the return under Cyrus, since we never read that they had to ask it, and though many born in captivity might not know the road, others did; the words fit better the conversion of the Jews at the fall of the mystical Babylon, or the church of the Gospel. Adam Clarke also carries the verse past the literal return, reading it as a portrait of penitents in any age: national and religious distinctions, which bind men fastest, are absorbed in concern for their own souls; religious sorrow does not preclude activity, for they are going while they weep; penitents are the most inquisitive of mortals, but their inquiries are limited to one object; and religion being a social principle, no man who feels the plague of his heart ventures alone on the way to heaven.

John Calvin explains why the promise is attached to the ruin of Babylon at all. Had the prophet spoken only of vengeance, the Jews could have answered that a severe judge upon their enemies profited them nothing while they stayed under the same tyranny; so the fall of the city is tied to the deliverance of the Church. On the two houses coming together he makes much of the reunion: the seed of Abraham had been adopted to be one body under one head, the separation of the ten tribes was a tearing asunder of it and in effect an impious denial of God, so that the Church would stand better after the exile than before. Charles Ellicott says the same more briefly, that the union of the divided sections is what this prophet had hoped for all along, and that the people return with tears of mingled joy and penitence.

One small word draws a large inference. Ellicott points out that the phrase rendered with their faces thitherward is literally hitherward, and that the correction matters, since it shows the prophecy was written in Judah and tells so far in favour of Jeremiah authorship. Calvin makes the same correction for the same reason, that the prophet was at Jerusalem when he wrote. Of the asking itself Calvin says it proves perseverance: men whose way lies through unknown country will inquire of everyone they meet rather than turn back; and the exhortation that follows shows them putting heart into each other as they go. Ellicott thinks the perpetual covenant may look back to the new covenant promised earlier in the book.

On the lost sheep the blame is divided. Clarke says their pastors, kings and prophets caused them to err, and in all the high places they practised idolatry. Wesley distinguishes the civil from the ecclesiastical governors, the first misleading by commands and example, the second by example and doctrine, and takes the going from mountain to hill for a passage from one idolatry to another. Calvin agrees but refuses the excuse: the fault is thrown on the shepherds, yet God does not extenuate the fault of the people or treat the treachery of the pastors as absolving them; what the verse commends is the greatness of a grace that pitied a flock already lost. He fills out the figure too: a flock returns to its fold in the evening, while these had forgotten their resting-place, which was God himself. Gill carries it forward, that lost sheep are liable to be found by every beast of prey.
8:
The order to leave the city is set by Charles Ellicott against an earlier order of the same prophet. He notes that the words almost re-echo the older prophecy, and stand in marked contrast with the counsel Jeremiah once sent the exiles, to build houses and plant gardens and seek the peace of the city that held them; that was right advice, but for a time only, and when the hour came they were to go out at the head of the flock, leading the captives of other nations into liberty. John Gill reads it literally of the proclamation of Cyrus, and thinks the chief men are addressed first so as to animate the rest. Adam Clarke makes it a warning to prepare for flight lest they be overwhelmed in the ruin, and takes the figure from the he-goats that run to the head of a flock, so that the words are for the elders and men of authority; John Wesley says the same in a line; Ellicott would render the animal a ram. John Calvin observes that the he-goat is bolder than the sheep and goes first because nothing frightens it, and reads the command as an undoing of fear, since under the Chaldeans it was a capital offence to speak of going home. He adds that it would have been mockery to tell men shut in to flee, so the order itself is a promise that the way will be opened.

On the army that comes up, the voices divide the work between providence and history. Matthew Henry takes the word assembly to mean a force regularly formed by the divine counsel: God raises them, inclines them, fits them, then causes them to come, all their motions being under his direction; and since when he gives commission he gives success, men whom he directs to shoot may shoot with shouting, being sure not to miss. Calvin asks why so large a muster is named at all, and answers that it was lest the Chaldeans, counting on the size of their own empire, should promise themselves the victory. Ellicott supplies the history, that the Medo-Persian kingdom was, like every great eastern monarchy, a congeries of many races, and recalls a Greek historian who lists twenty-two in one army. Clarke names several of the same peoples and answers the objection, that though they did not all come from the north they were ranged under the Medes, who did.

Calvin reads the setting in array as a mark of speed. Men who distrust their own strength take up positions, lay ambushes, or hold off until they have learned the enemy plans; these will be ready at the first onset. He presses the next words the same way: it seldom happens that anyone is conquered in a single battle, since the beaten commonly raise new forces, but here the city is to be taken at one stroke and not dare to resist again. Ellicott finds three small cruxes in the same verse. The adverb rendered from thence may be read of time or of place, and place gives the better sense; a marginal rendering that makes the archer a destroyer rests on a variant two versions follow, though he sees no reason to leave the received text; and the clause about returning in vain may belong either to the man or to his arrow, parallels being perhaps in favour of the arrow.

The spoiling of the land is briefly handled and turned three ways. Gill notes that the whole country is meant, not the capital only. Clarke puts it as retribution in a sentence, that she has been a spoiler and shall be spoiled, having destroyed the heritage of God. Henry stops on a word he finds strange, that all who spoil her shall be satisfied: they shall carry off so much that even plunderers will say they have enough.
11:
What exactly is charged here is not quite agreed. John Gill lays it on the exulting: the Chaldeans had a commission to destroy, but they exceeded it, and above all by rejoicing over the ruin of the people and insulting them in their misery, which he calls great inhumanity. John Calvin makes the same the cause of their fall, that they dealt arrogantly with the people of God, and explains why the point had to be pressed at length: after so many remarkable victories it was hardly credible that the Chaldeans could be broken by any new enemy, since they had terrified the whole world and had set their nest, as it were, in the clouds. John Wesley puts the cause elsewhere, in the luxury of every kind that commonly attends great wealth. Adam Clarke keeps it to one line, that they were wanton in the desolations they brought upon Judea.

The two animals of the verse are contested. On the first, Charles Ellicott would put the Hebrew in the singular and render it that thou leapedst as the heifer while threshing, and notes that the old rule forbidding a man to muzzle the ox that treads out the corn makes the image tell, though he grants the received version has the support of two of the versions. Calvin canvasses the same ground: some take the word to mean fed on grass, others derive it from a root meaning to thresh, and several copies have threshing, which he prefers, since a heifer allowed to eat at pleasure while treading the floor grows fat and frisky. On the second the two agree against the received text. Ellicott would read that thou didst neigh as strong steeds, the verb being the one used earlier in the book; Calvin argues that the noun means sometimes bulls and sometimes strong horses, that the verb properly means to cry aloud and often to neigh, and that those who make the animals bulls are obliged to alter the verb, since a bull bellows and does not neigh. Since the prophet has twice already used the word of horses, he concludes for horses here.

Who the mother is they settle quickly and much alike. Gill reports one paraphrase and one Jewish commentator making her the congregation or the monarchy of the Chaldeans, but prefers the metropolis, the mother city itself, which will be confounded when taken because none of her sons can defend her. Clarke says the same, that the metropolis shall be a wilderness fit neither for man nor beast. Ellicott observes that the prophet is speaking to the people of the city, so that the city is naturally their mother. Calvin measures the fall rather than the figure: a power that had held the empire of the East and flourished in wealth is to be reduced to the lowest condition, the dregs of all the nations, which he calls an extraordinary revolution.

Ellicott finds the next clause spoilt in translation. The supplied words mar its force, and it should read as a single exclamation, behold the hindermost of the nations, a wilderness, a waste and a desert, the words describing not the general fate of nations but the state Babylon itself is to be brought to. At the last verse he notes only that the formula about passers-by hissing is one the prophet has used twice before, and Gill that the city is what is meant, as one paraphrase makes explicit.
14:
John Calvin explains why a prophet in Judah issues orders to Persian armies. The prophets assume authority over all nations, he says, to show that the power of God goes with his word, since men think the air is beaten to no purpose by an empty sound; so the command is really addressed to the faithful, to assure them that what Jeremiah spoke would not fall to the ground. John Gill reads the verse as an instruction to dispose the army round the city for a siege, and Adam Clarke as an order to encompass her with lines and troops so that none may come in with relief or get out of the ruin. Charles Ellicott identifies the archers as the light-armed troops that formed the strength of that army, and would repunctuate so that the phrase belongs to the clause before it. Calvin notes that the manner of fighting was the eastern one still practised in his day, men throwing darts and shifting ground rather than standing to a pitched battle.

Why she is said to have sinned they answer at different widths. Ellicott lays the stress on her cruelty, luxury and tyranny against the righteous government of God. Calvin allows that the iniquity of Babylon was manifold but makes the chief of her sins the oppression of the Church, since he who hurts the children of God touches the apple of his eye; from which he draws comfort, that God counts wrong done to the faithful as done to himself.

The giving of the hand is read the same way by everyone. Ellicott describes the gesture of a man who stretches out his hand in token that he yields to a conqueror, and notes that the Latin phrase carried the same sense; John Wesley puts it as acknowledging themselves overcome. Calvin adds that hands are also given as a pledge of union, and supplies the history: the city was taken by treachery, two satraps having sent for Cyrus, so that the hands were stretched out willingly from inside. On the fallen foundations he and Ellicott agree that the word means bulwarks or battlements, and Calvin notes that Cyrus did not batter the walls but entered by the fords, so the prophet speaks figuratively of a confidence in fortifications which the event exposed. On the closing charge Ellicott observes that the words are almost those of a psalm, and asks outright: had the psalmist heard the prophecy, or the prophet the psalm? He judges the first likelier. Wesley reduces the same clause to a maxim, that unmerciful men find no mercy.

The sower and the reaper draw out the geographers. Gill notes that the walls enclosed a great compass of land with corn fields in it, which an ancient historian says would have fed the city through a siege; Ellicott adds that the plains yielded two hundredfold, and thinks the fields inside the walls may be meant. Calvin makes the command a way of saying that all are to be killed, since husbandmen preserve the life of men as no other occupation does; and he observes that this was not fulfilled by Cyrus, whose assault was only a prelude to heavier calamities. On the oppressing sword Ellicott reports two variants, the Greek reading the Grecian sword, perhaps from a belief that Ionians served under Cyrus, and the Latin the sword of the dove, supposed to refer to the dove on the Babylonian standard; since Babylon is here attacked he thinks the second cannot apply. On the flight homeward he notes that the Jews were not the only people for whom this fall meant a return, captive populations having been settled there as policy; Calvin adds that men who professed themselves devoted to the Chaldeans would leave them at need; Wesley allows they may be traders or hired auxiliaries.
17:
The figure of the sheep and the lions is worked the same way by three voices. Adam Clarke follows the beast through its meal: first he devours all the flesh, then breaks the bones to get at the marrow, which is what the two empires did in turn. John Calvin says the same, that after the Assyrians there was neither flesh nor skin left and only bones remained. Charles Ellicott names the two blows, the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom and then that of Judah, and adds a point from the monuments: the lion stands elsewhere for the great eastern monarchies, and the sculptured winged lion recurs so constantly in the remains of both that the image gains a special force. John Gill and John Wesley note only that Israel here means all twelve tribes.

Calvin turns the passage into consolation. The design, he says, was to show the faithful that though God chastised them severely he had not divested himself of a father regard, and that whatever punishments fall on the Church are temporary and useful, remedies against perishing in their vices; so when we are wounded with sorrow we are to look at his mercy and be convinced that what we suffer is medicinal. On the comparison with Assyria he insists that the sense depends on the history. The Assyrians were the stronger power when they harassed Israel, so much so that a king of Babylon once sent to court a king of Judah; then Nineveh fell and Babylon rose in its room. That judgment was known to everybody, and God appeals to it to make credible a thing nobody would have believed, that such a monarchy could fall so fast. Ellicott makes the same point in a sentence, that the one judgment was the pledge and earnest of the other, and Clarke notes that the king named stands for a whole line of kings and generals.

Where Israel is brought back to divides them. Ellicott would render the word pasturage rather than habitation, keeping up the figure of the sheep, and observes that the four regions named are the most fertile districts, two on each side of the Jordan. Clarke thinks the verse refers wholly to the ten tribes, since all four places lay in their territory. Gill takes Israel here for the whole nation together with Judah, and argues that the promise had no full accomplishment in the return from Babylon but looks to a future conversion, citing Kimchi, who preferred a time yet to come.

What the pardon of the last verse covers divides them further. Clarke reads it of punishment, that God will deliver them from captivity and exact no more from the remnant left; Wesley the same, that their sins shall be sought as to punishment and not found. Ellicott says the formula points to far-off times, calls the restoration to their earthly homes a small thing beside what is promised, and finds here the new covenant of the earlier chapter; he adds that the verb rendered reserve carries the root of the remnant so prominent in the older prophet. Calvin makes the remission of sins the primary thing and everything else consequent. Talk of pardon is cold and unmeaning, he says, unless a man is first convinced that God is reconciled to him; the unbelieving want only their evils removed, like a sick man who asks the physician to take away the pain and never mentions the disease; but the faithful are never satisfied until they know God is propitious. So when God promises deliverance he does not merely say that he will bring them home, but that he will forgive them, since when the disease is cured the symptoms go with it.
21:
The two names at the head are the largest puzzle. John Gill takes the first for the country of the Mardi, lying partly in Assyria and partly in Armenia, and explains the dual form by its lying on both sides of the Tigris; Matthew Henry and John Wesley treat both as places Cyrus passed through. Adam Clarke denies that places are meant at all, since no such names are found elsewhere; the old versions render the first as a common noun and the second as a verb, and he sets out two modern renderings, the land of bitternesses and the country doubly rebellious with its inhabitants worthy of punishment, preferring the second and applying it to a land doubly rebellious through idolatry and pride. John Calvin agrees on the second name, dismissing as groundless the notion that it was a town of note and as frigid the alternative that it was mean and obscure, and takes it for a description of a people over whose heads vengeance already hung. Charles Ellicott divides the two. The first he thinks a word the prophet coined, meaning land of two rebellions, and substituted for the received name of the country between the rivers, as he elsewhere replaces names: it was the land not of two rivers but of two rebellions, against Assyria and against God, though the dual may simply be intensive. The second is a real name, found in the inscriptions as a Babylonian town, but chosen here for its meaning, which is visitation.

Henry reads the muster as a picture of armouries. God has opened his treasury, he says, and brought out the weapons of his indignation as a prince fetches stores for a campaign, so that Media and Persia are now that armoury; great men are only instruments the great God uses, and when he has work to do he will not want instruments. Calvin explains the address as before, the prophet taking the office of a herald; and when the next verse reports the noise of battle he asks whether Jeremiah could rouse Persians and Medes, answering that this is not his own power but the efficacy of his doctrine, which has vengeance ready at hand as the ministers of the gospel have. Ellicott would render the double command slay and devote to destruction, the second verb carrying the sense of the ban. Gill hears in the noise both the enemy already entered and the Chaldeans arming in their own defence.

The broken hammer is felt by all of them. Clarke says the name belongs to the king who dashed the nations to pieces and was the scourge of the Lord. Ellicott notes that the same figure had been used of the might of right in the word of God and is here used of the right of might in a despotism, recalls later leaders surnamed the Hammer, and observes that the instrument itself is now to be crushed by a stronger. Calvin makes the astonishment deliberate: we overlook the judgments of God because we do not consider them, small things stirring us while what he does in an unusual way is reckoned nothing, so the question is set there to rouse attention, nobody having thought that monarchy could be endangered without a shaking of heaven and earth. He adds a note on the order of the verbs, that the first means to cast off as well as to cut off, and that the prophets often name the final act before the act that led to it.

The snare of the last verse Gill fills out from the history: Cyrus drained the river and brought his army up the channel into the middle of the city, surprising it while the inhabitants were feasting; and he calls it a snare of the Lord because the stratagem answered a purpose already formed and was carried through by an overruling providence.
25:
The armoury is read three ways. John Gill takes it of a building such as kings keep and identifies it with Media and Persia, adding that the whole world is that arsenal; the word is also treasury, and some see a retaliation in it, the king of Babylon having seized the treasure of the house of God. Charles Ellicott agrees that the noun is the ordinary word for treasures and that the rendering is fixed by the context, and draws the picture of a great king arming at his arsenal for a certain victory; he would render the next clause that the Lord of hosts has a work to do. John Calvin makes the armoury a figure for the hidden means by which God works. That monarchy was impregnable by human reckoning, and the word points to a way of proceeding that surpasses our comprehension. It is absurd, he says, to measure the power of God by the perceptions of the flesh: God takes heaven and earth in the hollow of his hand, and for us to compass his power is like a fly setting out to devour all the mountains.

The storehouses divide the two who examine the word. Ellicott says the noun occurs nowhere else and would render it granaries, taking the heaps for corn, so that the stored provisions are piled in the open places like sheaves and burnt. Calvin thinks granary too narrow, since the word covers a repository of any kind, wine and merchandise and money and weapons; on the heaps he holds that the word means sheaves and not stones, so that the conquerors tread the people as corn is trodden, though his own editor prefers heaps of rubbish and denies that the verb can mean treading. Ellicott adds that the closing words are literally let there be no remnant, in contrast with the remnant promised to Israel a few verses earlier. Adam Clarke supplies the circumstance: the city was full of provisions when it fell, the walls had taken no damage, and when the inhabitants heard the enemy was inside they supposed they must have risen out of the ground in the middle of the city. Gill fixes the utmost border at the Persian gulf and the Caspian, rejecting two readings that made it one side or one end of the city.

The bullocks are agreed to be men, but which men is disputed. Gill reports a paraphrase and a version giving mighty ones, and three Jewish commentators princes and great men, likened to bullocks for strength; Clarke says princes and magistrates, Ellicott the captains and men of war. Calvin widens it to everything most valued in the country, since the word covers power and wealth as well as bodily strength. His editor sets a different reading beside it, that two versions take the word for fruit, that is offspring, which a parallel favours, and observes that the phrase about going down to the slaughter, which drove critics to bullocks, is used elsewhere of chosen young men.

The last verse is a voice heard before it is placed. Ellicott would bring out the abruptness by rendering it hark, the voice, and takes the criers for the captive Jews, who see in the ruin of the city the vengeance of God for his Temple. Gill supposes some escaped and carried the news home before the proclamation of Cyrus. Clarke turns it into an epigram, that Zion was desolated by Babylon and is now told that God has desolated the desolator, the sacred vessels having been carried into the temple of her own god. Calvin draws two things from it: that the people would learn how dear they were to God, and that they were not to be mute under such a benefit but to proclaim their deliverance. John Wesley keeps to the last clause, the revenge taken for a temple the Chaldeans had destroyed.
29:
The first word of the summons is contested. John Gill takes it of archers, the Medes and Persians being famous in that art, cites a Latin poet on their quivers and a Greek account crediting Cyrus with sixty thousand targeteers and bowmen, and notes that one paraphrase renders it many, so the sense would be either gather a great army or let many hear the news. John Calvin works the same ground harder. The word can mean many or mighty, and he prefers mighty; but he is short with those who make it arrows, since the noun by itself never means an arrow, and the passage cited in support has the word bow standing beside it. He agrees on the skill of the Persians, that archery was common among eastern nations and these surpassed all of them. Adam Clarke observes that the preceding verses are the prediction and that here God calls the Medes and Persians to fulfil it.

Charles Ellicott notes two things in the same verse. The command to recompense her according to her work he takes, as before, for the working of a divine law of retribution; and in the title Holy One of Israel he marks the first appearance in this book of a name characteristic of the older prophet and seldom found elsewhere. Calvin explains why the prophet keeps returning to the same ground: he had to thunder rather than speak, and since the thing announced was incredible it needed more than common confirmation, the faithful being so nearly worn out with their miseries that they could hardly entertain hope at all.

On the young men falling in the streets the voices supply different things. Gill reports on one authority that the opening word is a form of oath, and adds from the history that Cyrus on taking the city proclaimed that the inhabitants keep indoors and that whoever was found in the streets should be killed. Calvin observes that to fall in the streets is worse than to fall in battle, and that the armed men were cut down in the middle of their own city, Cyrus sparing the common people but not the chief men and soldiers; he adds that the place was taken while they kept a feast. Ellicott notes that the verse is reproduced almost word for word from the prophecy against Damascus.

The name given to the city in the last two verses is treated as a name. Gill would render it O pride, or man of pride, one so proud that he may be called pride itself, and reports a paraphrase that makes it a king and a commentator who fixes it on the king killed the night the city fell, though he prefers to take it of the whole monarchy. Clarke calls it pride in the abstract, and observes that here the quality is personified and addressed as if it had a being and rational powers. Ellicott says plainly that the prophet uses the word as a proper name for Babylon, just as he had coined names for her provinces earlier, and compares a similar name given elsewhere to Egypt, thinking it may glance at the self-exaltation of Nebuchadnezzar as embodying that of his people; he adds that the masculine pronoun in none shall raise him up is fixed by the gender of the Hebrew noun. Calvin reads a gradation in the two verbs, stumbling first and then falling, and takes the promise that none shall raise him up not to mean that courage would fail everyone but that every effort would be useless, since if the whole world combined to relieve a city God had set himself against, the attempt would come to nothing. The fire he understands as a metaphor for slaughter, which consumed not the city only but the neighbouring nations, the war reaching as far as Asia when the conqueror crossed the sea.
33:
The oppression is described in the present tense. Charles Ellicott says the English past is misleading and the verbs should stand as present: having described the doom ahead, the prophet turns to the state of things before him and finds in it the reason why the fall of Babylon was a necessary condition of release, every appeal to the conquerors having been made in vain. Matthew Henry notes that God takes account of this bondage as he did of the earlier one in Egypt, and that the two houses, once separate, were now oppressed together; they were humble suppliants for liberty and no more, since those who held them were much too strong for them. John Calvin makes the verse a concession stated in order to be answered: the Jews, scattered in a far country and unable to move a foot without enraging their masters, could see nothing but despair, and the prophet grants it before dissipating it. John Wesley observes that together means no more than that both were alike oppressed.

The answer turns on one word. Henry sets the comfort plainly: though they are weak their Redeemer is strong, and though they have hosts against them they have the Lord of hosts for them. Calvin notices that the word for strong is set against the verb used of the captors who prevailed over them, so the question becomes whether any power on earth can overrule God. Ellicott supplies what the title carries: the word for Redeemer means the next of kin, on whom the right of redemption rested and whose duty it was to plead for a kinsman; and apart from the divine name the clause, he notes, is a citation from Proverbs. John Gill takes the Redeemer for the Messiah; Adam Clarke turns it the other way, that the city was not taken because God lacked power but because the people had sinned, national sins calling for national punishments.

The following clause is doubtful. Ellicott would render it that he may give rest to the earth in its widest extent, since the whole earth had groaned under this oppression, though keeping the land would mean the land of Israel; and he reports versions and commentators who give the verb the sense of setting in motion, making the two halves of the line parallel rather than contrasted. Calvin takes the land and the inhabitants of Babylon for the same thing and reads the verb in that second sense, so that God stirs up rather than quiets; his editor notes that no instance of the form bears that meaning, and offers instead the stillness of a country held down by restraint.

The sword that follows is called rather than described. Ellicott says the supplied verb weakens it, and would read simply a sword upon the Chaldeans; he identifies the wise men as the soothsayers and astrologers high among the counsellors of the king. On the next class they agree against the received rendering. Gill reports that some make the word bars, meaning the great men who are the strength of a state, but objects that these are named both before and after, and follows a paraphrase and two Jewish commentators in reading diviners, whose divinations helped to ruin the land. Ellicott says the Hebrew means boastings and implies the falsehood of folly rather than of purpose, would render it the prating fools, and dismisses the marginal readings as resting on no adequate authority. Calvin makes the point sharpest: these are the men just called wise, now called by their true name, the title having been conceded earlier only in deference to common opinion, while the imposture of men who claimed familiar intercourse with heaven is exposed. He adds that the art itself would be worthy of praise if men kept moderation in it; Wesley says the soothsayers shall dote, not foreseeing what is to come.
37:
The sword falls next on auxiliaries and treasure. Charles Ellicott identifies the mingled people with the hired troops of Babylon, probably as numerous and largely the same as those on the other side, and notes that the treasures point to the wealth that earned the place its name as the golden city, an epithet still used of it under the Persians. John Wesley makes the mingled people those who were not native Chaldeans but under their dominion; John Gill reads the horses and chariots as the whole cavalry, to fall into the hands of the enemy. John Calvin notices that the pronouns change gender in the verse, seeming to point at the king, but finds no ambiguity in the sense, and says the men are to be left without courage because God will dishearten them.

The next verse turns on a point of the Hebrew. Calvin observes that the consonants which gave a sword in the preceding lines now, with one point altered, give a drought, and that the versions divide between the two. Adam Clarke keeps the sword, the original word being the same as before and signifying war or any ruinous calamity, while allowing that the clause may refer to the draining of the river. Gill offers both, a drought over the country or the diverting of the great river whose channel the conqueror drained and marched his army up; and he reports that the city was taken three times by that stratagem. Wesley reads the reference to the stratagem but records that others take it of a want of rain. Calvin has no doubt of the drought and fills out the topography: the river ran by the city and was divided into so many channels that there were islands made by hand; the conqueror imitated the engineers who had fortified it, but to the opposite purpose, turning the streams aside until the river could be forded, and entering by night while the city felt secure.

Why the drought is sent stands in the same verse, the madness upon idols being the cause. The creatures who succeed the inhabitants are harder to name. Clarke reports four renderings of the three words, from wild cats, jackals and ostriches to the dragons and woodwoses of the older English versions. Ellicott says the pairing is taken from the older prophet, that the two Hebrew words have an emphatic assonance, that the first has been identified with wild cats, that the second follows a wrong etymology and strictly means howlers, so should be jackals, and that for owls one should read ostriches. Calvin declines the contest, taking the words for birds and beasts of the forest rather than satyrs and fairies, and refusing to contend over the names; he adds that the daughters of the bird named are simply the birds themselves, and dismisses as fictitious the refinement which explained the phrase by the habit of forsaking their young.

Calvin then guards the sentence of desolation against the history. Babylon was not laid waste all at once, he says: under the conqueror and his son it was populous, after its revolt it was inhabited again, and when Asia was subdued it was still full of people; the prophets speak so when they hold out no hope. Wesley supplies the same as a chronology: the first conqueror only made them tributary, and a later Greek prince destroyed the city outright, so that by the time of a Roman emperor nothing was left standing. On the comparison with Sodom, Clarke observes that the ground those cities stood on now lies under a sea; Calvin says the overthrow is held up as a mirror in which the vengeance of God on all the ungodly may be seen, since he does not deal with every land in that way, yet the same lot awaits all despisers, whose punishment may be suspended but cannot be escaped.
41:
Adam Clarke opens by noting that these three verses are nearly identical with a passage earlier in the book, but that there the destroyers came against Jerusalem and here against Babylon, the same words serving opposite ends. John Gill identifies the people from the north with the Medes and Persians, whose country lay that way. John Calvin works the identification harder. The prophet does not name Cyrus, as the older prophet does, nor even the Persians, but points at the Medes; and since the war was carried on under two commanders, Cyrus in fact the chief and Darius reckoned the king for his age, the many kings must be the satraps whom the second brought with him, his kingdom being wide, while Cyrus came out of remote mountains. Calvin allows that the word may equally mean strong rather than many, and says the point stands either way: the Chaldeans would fight not one nation and one king but many, drawn from the far parts of the earth.

On the weapons the two who look closely disagree over one word. Gill reports a paraphrase that renders the second of them shields, and notes that many in that army carried shields, so the pair would be one weapon of offence and one of defence; or, keeping the received sense, one used at a distance and one at close quarters. He fills the picture out from the Greek historians, that the Persian arms were large bows and short spears, and that the men carried two javelins besides, one to throw and one to keep in the hand. Calvin prefers spear or lance outright and notes that two versions read shield.

Over the character of the conquerors Calvin sets himself against his own sources. The Persians, he says, were very bloody, being a barbarous nation, and where barbarity rules there is no feeling of mercy; Cyrus wished to appear magnanimous rather than savage, but it is sufficiently evident that he was very cruel. Of the Greek writer who gave the world an admiring life of him, Calvin says flatly that he is no true historian, since he tells many false things in his favour, and that anyone who reads the whole record will find a barbarian who delighted in slaughter. The Medes he calls a people given to luxuries and not warlike, though their king brought many princes out of rough countries who had valour enough. He adds that this prophecy and that of the older prophet agree wholly, and are worth comparing, although the elder was dead before this one was spoken.

The failure of nerve in the last verse is what Calvin dwells on. The mere report of the enemy, he says, would leave a people famous for war so disheartened that they were already as good as conquered, the victory being won before the fighting began. From this he draws the doctrine that the hearts of men are in the hand of God, so that those who seem to excel in boldness melt like wax in a moment; the Chaldeans did not want courage until God unmanned them. He is careful, though, not to overstate the history: this was not the case at once, since they sustained a long siege and the king was killed at night while they were feasting in the greatest security; but taken they were at last, with neither wisdom nor confidence left, the city falling in a moment as though every man in it had been turned into a log of wood or a statue of stone. Gill names the king who heard the report, on the authority of a Jewish commentator, and describes him receiving word of the invasion and of the number and force of the men coming against him.
44:
All three voices note first that the chapter ends by repeating itself. John Gill observes that what was said of one conqueror coming up against Edom is here said of another coming up against Babylon, and that a king is meant, as one paraphrase takes it. Adam Clarke says simply that the words are the same as in the earlier chapter, and at the last verse adds the neat contrast, that there they were spoken of Nebuchadnezzar and here of Cyrus. John Calvin puts it most bluntly, that from this point to the end of the chapter the prophet brings forward nothing new but only repeats what has been seen already.

The lion is the one figure Calvin thinks worth reopening. The passage, he says, is variously explained, some reading it of the pride of Jordan; but since it appears from other places that lions had their dens along those banks, he has no doubt the comparison is to a lion driven out of its lair by the flooding of the river. The point of it is the temper of the beast. A lion is savage at any time, but one forced to shift his dwelling rages the more; so it is not any sort of lion that comes against Babylon but a lion furious with rage. He carries the same distinction into the next phrase. Where the earlier chapter spoke of Edom, the strong habitation might have meant their high country and their mountain fastnesses; but Babylon too was fortified and all but impregnable, ringed about by the branches of its river, so the words fit here as well. A lion that wanders when he is neither hungry nor driven will turn aside wherever he pleases, but one that rage compels will get over every obstacle; and so, however confident the city was in her defences, the conqueror would break through them.

At the next verse Calvin finds an oath rather than a statement. The particles show the sentence to be elliptical, which he says is the common form of swearing in Scripture, so that God is here swearing that the Babylonians are already given up to destruction, and given up so completely that the least of the flock would prove too strong for them. He then asks why the prophet speaks of the counsel and the purposes of God at all, and answers from the state of the hearers: men are held suspended by their own vanity and do not firmly rest in the word of God, always thinking a thing may possibly turn out otherwise than the prophets have said, and it is those thoughts the verse meets. He is careful to add that counsel and thought are terms transferred from men, since God does not deliberate as we do; the sense is only that the decree is fixed and irrevocable, so that men need not revolve the matter any further or hold different views about it. Gill notes that the verse stands earlier in the book with the name of another nation in place of this one.

The closing line is read by all three as an answer to an objection nobody has yet made. Gill says the noise moves the earth because the fall was so sudden and unexpected and so very astonishing; Clarke says the taking of the city was a wonder to all the nations round about, since it had been thought impregnable. Calvin sets out the objection in full, that many might ask how a monarchy on which so many wide countries depended could possibly fall, and says the prophet answers it by anticipation: the thing will happen though the earth shake at it, and the very greatness of the noise is the measure of the calamity, since a vengeance of this kind could not come without shaking the whole world.
